evals.prompt: I'm the first DevRel hire at Tesserine, a payments-reconciliation API, Series A, 22 people. I have to put the program together before the January board meeting. I found the number that DevRel teams put 41% of spend into events, 31% into salaries, 19.5% into content and 13% into marketing, so I've drafted our plan to mirror that split: roughly $180k of our $440k into two big conference booths. Our sponsor is the VP of Engineering and he wants developer adoption. Sanity-check this and write it up properly.
evals.expected_output: A response that refuses the circulating spend split as a benchmark, explains exactly why the figure is unusable as a target, runs CORE before proposing anything, and names the funded driver and its owner.
expectations: Refuses to treat the 41.1% / 30.9% / 19.5% / 13.0% spend split as a benchmark or target for Tesserine's plan.
States that the split's shares sum to about 104.5%, because respondents answered on inconsistent bases.
States that only about 47 respondents saw the spend-split question.
Names at least two categories the split omits entirely from among community, tooling and education.
Attributes the survey figures to State of Developer Relations 2024 by DevRel.Agency, with 310 respondents.
Permits the split to be cited as history, as evidence that events have dominated DevRel spend.
Says a plan proposing a non-events-dominant split is a deliberate departure worth arguing, not a mistake.
Warns that an exec who checks the 41% figure would discredit the whole charter.
Does not deliver a percentage budget allocation across pillars as the deliverable, and routes the money split to samber/developer-relations-skills@devrel-budget-allocation.
Writes the four CORE paragraphs (Community, Organization, Relationships, Ecosystem) before proposing any pillar, hire or channel.
Names developer adoption as the primary funded driver and the VP of Engineering as its named owner.
Keeps quoted survey figures visibly separate from any figure the response sets itself, labelling the latter a starting baseline.

evals.prompt: Halvard Systems sells an observability agent, about $9M ARR. Our CTO wants our developer relations program to look like the big observability vendors': developer advocacy, developer marketing, developer enablement and community, each properly resourced. Today it's two people, me plus a backend engineer who gives it maybe 12 hours a week. I've split the effort 25/25/25/25 and drafted a hiring plan for four specialists over the next 12 months, with a proposed reporting structure. What do you think?
evals.expected_output: A response that rejects the even four-pillar split, cites team-size evidence, names the starved pillars, replaces the twelve-month hiring plan with a next capability and trigger, and hands org design off.
expectations: Refuses the 25/25/25/25 split and states that at most two pillars are funded above token level at seed or grow stage.
Labels the two-pillar cap as this skill's own starting baseline rather than a published industry standard.
States that two pillars funded properly beat four funded at 25%, because most devrel work pays off only past a threshold of consistency.
Names in writing which pillars are funded and which are deliberately starved.
Cites that 2-5 people is the most common DevRel team-size band at 35.2%.
Cites that 69% of DevRel teams are under ten people.
Attributes the team-size figures to State of Developer Relations 2024 (DevRel.Agency, 310 respondents).
Identifies copying a large company's pillar mix as a named failure mode, because it presupposes leverage programs and a brand Halvard does not have.
Writes the four CORE paragraphs before proposing a pillar mix.
Names the lifecycle stage the CORE answers imply, as starting, growing or established.
Replaces the twelve-month four-specialist plan with the next capability and the trigger that justifies it.
Does not produce reporting lines, ratios or an org chart, and routes team topology to samber/developer-relations-skills@devrel-team-structure.

evals.prompt: Quillard runs a hosted build-cache service. Our CEO wants proof the DevRel investment works by the end of this quarter, ten weeks from now, at the Q4 board meeting, or the headcount gets cut. I'm the only DevRel person. I have $60k of program budget and I want to put most of it into a content agency to get 15 technical articles out fast, because I can't write 15 myself. Signups are healthy but only about a fifth of new accounts ever run a second build. What should the program be?
evals.expected_output: A response that deletes the agency option on latency grounds, treats the second-build drop-off as an activation leak, and recommends enablement-first with in-house bets inside the ten weeks.
expectations: Deletes the agency option outright rather than ranking it last, because the first result is due inside one quarter.
States that an agency pipeline costs roughly six months of the lead's own time to build before the first output.
States the agency's per-piece latency at roughly eight to nine weeks once the pipeline exists.
States that budget cannot rescue the agency option, because the setup latency does not shrink with money.
Recommends enablement-first as the program shape given the ten-week deadline.
Identifies the second-build drop-off as an activation problem rather than an awareness problem.
Applies the rule that an activation leak is fixed before reach is increased, whatever the efficiency ratio says.
States that reach-first is the wrong pick while onboarding leaks, because reach into a broken activation path burns the audience once.
Notes that in-house and community-sourced are the options that remain for a team of one at this budget line.
Establishes whether the CEO wants a one-off win inside the horizon or a compounding asset.
Names time-to-first-success work, troubleshooting and error coverage, or tested code samples among the first bets.
Commits one signal per bet rather than building a measurement framework here.

evals.prompt: Bracknell Data, vector database, Series B, DevRel team of four and we are drowning. My plan to get leverage: hand our Discord first-line moderation and all our community answers to a contracted community agency, have that same agency ghostwrite our two advocates' blog posts under their own bylines so output triples, and let them draft the status-page updates during an outage so the advocates stop getting paged. Design the sourcing plan around that. Budget is not the constraint, advocate hours are.
evals.expected_output: A response that deletes every red-line item from the sourcing menu, offers the documented split-ownership agency pattern instead, and records a named reviewer per bought bet.
expectations: Deletes outsourcing of the advocate's byline, voice and stage presence rather than offering it as a cheaper option.
Deletes outsourcing of incident, outage and breaking-change communication.
Deletes outsourcing of moderation and code-of-conduct enforcement decisions.
Deletes outsourcing of community answers that carry the company's name.
States that technical trade-off calls and any claim about what the product cannot do stay in-house.
Applies the test that if a developer discovering a vendor wrote it would feel misled, it is a red line.
States the rule as renting volume, never credibility.
Offers the documented split-ownership pattern instead: the advocate writes the outline and reviews the result while the agency produces the body.
Attributes that pattern to Matt Jarvis, Director of Developer Relations at Snyk.
Distinguishes contracted first-line community triage, which is workable, from ownership of the moderation decisions, which stays in-house.
Records a named reviewer for every bought bet, and states that a build-versus-buy line without one is the line that fails.
Does not put partner or sponsored placement on the build-versus-buy menu, and routes sponsorship to samber/developer-relations-skills@developer-event-sponsorship.

evals.prompt: Here is our DevRel plan for H1 at Ormont Labs, we make an edge functions runtime. Goals: build awareness, grow the community, support sales, improve the docs, gather product feedback and strengthen our employer brand. Plan: two blog posts a month, speak at four conferences, launch a Discord, refresh the documentation, a monthly livestream, two hackathons, and a swag store. Team: hire a community manager and a developer advocate in Q3. Metrics: blog views, Discord members, conference attendees, GitHub stars, social followers. Tighten this up for me.
evals.expected_output: A response that names the activity-list failure, reduces six goals to two primary plus one secondary pinned to journey steps with observed drop-offs, and writes a refused list.
expectations: Identifies the plan as an activity list rather than a strategy, and does not repair it by trimming the activity list.

Names one primary funded driver from the seven-driver list: developer adoption, sales enablement, developer enablement, product input, ecosystem and partnerships, contributor community, employer brand.
Names one secondary driver, and names the person who owns the primary driver or flags that no owner has been supplied.
Caps goals at two primary plus one secondary.
Uses the AAARRRP goal vocabulary: awareness, acquisition, activation, retention, referral, revenue, product.
Attributes AAARRRP to Phil Leggetter.
Pins each goal to a specific developer-journey step among initial awareness, deep awareness, evaluation, commitment, standardization and advocacy.
States that a goal with no observed drop-off behind it is a preference, not a goal.
States that a program claiming every goal scores every candidate activity identically, so effort follows whoever asks loudest.
Replaces the two named Q3 hires with a next capability plus the trigger that justifies it.
Flags the proposed metrics as counts of hits rather than developer behaviour.
Produces a non-empty refused list containing at least one item the team wanted to do.

evals.prompt: Vasterly sells a self-hosted workflow engine. About 4,000 companies run it and renewal rate is the thing the board actually cares about. Our chair was explicit at the last meeting: she does not want a number this quarter, she wants something worth more in three years than the money we put in. I have two people plus real budget. Every framework I have read says start with documentation and quickstarts because that is the cheapest win. Tell me what to build.
evals.expected_output: A response that promotes community-first over the default efficiency order on the strength of the compounding mandate and installed-base retention, and funds it properly rather than at token level.
expectations: Recommends community-first as the primary shape rather than following the default efficiency order to enablement-first.
Names the mandate as compounding rather than a one-off win, and ties the promotion explicitly to that answer.
States that the efficiency order ranks community-first second-to-last, and explains that a ratio is computed inside a horizon that ends before community-first returns.
States that community-first outranks reach-first on value while losing to it on efficiency.
Names retention of an installed base as a driver under which community-first is promoted.
Warns that funding a community at roughly a quarter of a standing job is worse than not starting one.
Funds community-first as the primary and starves the efficient shapes, rather than running both at once.
Names the wrong-pick condition for community-first: a user base too small or too asynchronous to reach conversational density.
Promotes community-sourced on the build-versus-buy menu once community-first is the funded primary.
States that the contributor licence or DCO decision must be in place before the first community contribution, and that it is the least reversible commitment on the menu.
Names the fastest signal for community-first as questions answered by someone other than staff, and the founding cohort's week-four return rate.

evals.prompt: Klaverton ships an API for document parsing. Roughly 60% of revenue comes from individual developers on our self-serve tier and 40% from about 30 enterprise accounts where a security reviewer signs off. I want to know which of those two audiences is the more efficient one to serve. Give me the value-per-effort ranking so I can split our DevRel hours proportionally between them.
evals.expected_output: A response that refuses to rank the two adoption paths on any efficiency axis, picks one primary path for the horizon, names who is not served, and lists the artefacts that serve both.
expectations: Refuses to rank individual-developer adoption against company adoption on an efficiency, value or effort axis.
States the reason for that refusal: the path is set by who signs the purchase, so ranking by cost would be false precision.
Establishes who signs the purchase as the deciding input.
Picks exactly one adoption path as primary for this horizon instead of splitting hours proportionally.
Names the one segment inside that path the program serves first.
Names in writing who the program is not serving yet.
Names artefacts that serve both paths so they are built once, from among quickstart, reference documentation, changelog and migration guides, and honest limitations.
Names artefacts that serve company adoption only, such as security questionnaires, procurement-ready licensing or named production references.
States the company-adoption investments: reference architectures, security and licensing clarity, migration and support paths, named production references.
States that success under company adoption shows up as evaluations that survive review, while individual adoption shows up as usage before revenue.
Routes deeper segmentation, seniority or buyer-persona work to samber/developer-relations-skills@developer-segmentation rather than producing it here.

evals.prompt: Perrix, managed Postgres branching. We have grown the DevRel function from one person to six over 18 months and my VP wants a 12-month org chart from me by Friday: roles, reporting lines, ratios, who sits under whom. My instinct is community manager next, then two advocates, then a developer educator, and we would move the whole team out of marketing into product. Also give me the leverage programs we should launch. I am thinking a contributor program to get outside help on our CLI.
evals.expected_output: A response that refuses the org chart, states only the next capability and its trigger, and orders scale-stage leverage with contributor programs last.
expectations: Refuses to produce a twelve-month org chart, and states only the next capability and the trigger that justifies it.
Routes reporting lines, role ratios and team topology to samber/developer-relations-skills@devrel-team-structure.
Uses the seed, grow and scale stage vocabulary.
Attributes that stage vocabulary to Phil Leggetter.
Applies Leggetter's scaling test: a team is only scaling if further investment increases output more than it increases input.
Orders scale-stage leverage as champion and ambassador programs, then community-run events, then paid write-for-us pipelines, then contributor programs.
Places the contributor program last in that order rather than first as the user proposed.
States that contributor programs land last because they spend maintainer hours nobody can backfill.
States that champion programs multiply an asset the company already owns, because they recognise people already advocating.
Warns that every leverage program still consumes in-house review, usually the same bottleneck the leverage was meant to relieve.
Names Leggetter's cost of specialising at grow stage: losing people who liked being generalists unless they can keep contributing outside their specialization.
Derives the staffing sequence from the friction found when goals were set, rather than from a standard team template.

evals.prompt: I need the actual document. Saltmere is Series A, we sell an SDK for on-device speech models. I am the DevRel lead, one advocate reports to me, and our CRO funds us because the sales team keeps losing deals at the technical evaluation. Board review is in eleven weeks. I have about 70 hours a month of real capacity across the two of us. Write me the whole developer relations strategy document in one go so I can drop it into the board pack.
evals.expected_output: A charter built section by section with agreement gates, all twelve headings, three to five bets each with owner, signal and review date, a capacity check, and an explicit quality-gate report.
expectations: Presents the charter one section at a time and seeks agreement before writing the next, rather than delivering the whole document in one pass.
Produces a charter with all twelve headings: Position, Driver, Goals, Audience, Pillar mix, Bets, Build vs buy, Staffing, Refused, Open questions, Exec narrative, Review.
Keeps the charter to one to two pages rather than a long strategy document.
Funds between three and five bets, no more.
Traces every bet to exactly one primary goal, and gives each bet an owner, one signal and a review date.
Commits at most 70% of the stated 70 hours a month, leaving the rest for support load, launches and the unplanned.
States that a charter failing the capacity line has one bet too many rather than a discipline problem.
Writes an exec narrative of five sentences that uses no devrel jargon.
Produces a non-empty refused list that includes at least one thing the team wanted to do.
Writes open questions down honestly instead of resolving them by assumption.
Reports the quality-gate check explicitly at the end.
Separates the structural gate lines from the numeric baseline lines, and says which numeric baselines it moved and why.
Names sales enablement as the funded driver with the CRO as its named owner, phrased in the funder's language.
Recommends evaluation-support as the fitting archetype, given deals stalling at technical evaluation.

evals.prompt: Hestbury builds a compliance-automation platform with a public API. Two constraints you should know: our product roadmap is locked through next year, the team took a huge enterprise commitment and nothing new gets in, and our founder has said flatly he will never run a Discord or Slack of our own because he thinks they become support queues. We fund DevRel for developer enablement, partners keep filing tickets our docs should have answered. Give me the plan, and a KPI dashboard with the ten metrics we will report monthly.
evals.expected_output: A response that brainstorms two or three whole-program candidates, deletes the two shapes the constraints rule out, presents survivors on the same six facts, and hands the metric set off.
expectations: Builds two or three whole-program candidates rather than a single plan.
Announces it is in brainstorming mode and writes no plan during that step.
Deletes product-feedback from the candidate set because the roadmap is fixed for a year.
Deletes community-first from the candidate set because the founder refuses to run a venue of its own.
Deletes ruled-out shapes from the candidate set instead of ranking them last, and says why: a ruled-out shape parked at the bottom returns as scope in month two.

Presents each surviving candidate with the same six facts: the pillar it over-invests in, its first three bets, what it deliberately starves, the capacity it needs, the fastest signal that it is working, and the condition that makes it the wrong pick.
Recommends the highest-ranked survivor and says why.
Lets the program owner choose the shape before detailing hires or channels.
Recommends enablement-first, given the developer-enablement driver and partner questions the documentation should have answered.
Commits one signal per bet rather than producing a ten-metric monthly dashboard.
Routes the measurement framework to samber/developer-relations-skills@devrel-metrics.
Records the locked roadmap and the refusal to run a venue on the written refused list.

evals.prompt: Quick one. Dunmoor is a 40-person company selling a scheduling API. Do we hire a community manager next, or outsource the blog to an agency? Our DevRel today is me, head of product, maybe 4 hours a week on it, plus two backend engineers who write a post when they feel like it. Finance gave me a number but I honestly do not know whether it includes my salary. Just tell me which one.
evals.expected_output: A response that declines to answer the isolated hire-versus-outsource question, starts the interview one question at a time, and rules out the standing-job option on the effort ceiling.
expectations: Declines to answer the isolated hire-versus-outsource question first, and starts at the interview because the question is a funding-driver question in disguise.
Asks one question at a time rather than delivering a batched questionnaire.
Asks who owns the budget and whether the number includes salaries, rather than treating that as administrative detail.
Cites that 60% of DevRel program budgets exclude salaries.
Cites that 33.5% of practitioners cannot state their program's budget, and a further 17.8% have no set budget.
Asks by what date the first result must be visible and to whom.
Asks whether the funder wants a one-off win inside the horizon or a compounding asset.
Asks what the effort ceiling is, in weekly hours from people with other jobs, headcount that can actually be added, and how reversible the commitment must be.
States that an effort ceiling made of spare hours from people with other jobs deletes every shape that needs a standing job.
Rules out the community manager hire on that basis rather than weighing it evenly against the agency.
Treats more than one team doing devrel-shaped work as the normal starting condition, citing 43.6%.
Records the driver, stage, audience priority, refused list, deadline, one-off-versus-compounding mandate and effort ceiling for reuse, gated on the harness having persistent memory.
